newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb jury in second day of deliberations.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb jury in second day of deliberations.

text.p: The jury in the trial of alleged Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh deliberated for a second day on Saturday, trying to decide whether the Gulf War veteran is a cold-blooded killer or a man wrongly accused.
The jury of seven men and five women arrived at the federal courthouse in Denver in two vans with darkened windows.
The wait for a verdict was already beginning to tell on relatives of bombing victims.

"We're all kind of tensed up, waiting for a guilty verdict. If it doesn't come back by Sunday night, then maybe we've got some people on the jury trying to look at the evidence in a different way," Charles Tomlin, whose son Rick died in the bombing, said.
Several hundred journalists kept watch at the federal courthouse in Denver, which was ringed by tight security, as it has been throughout the high-profile trial.
The jury spent nearly a full day on Friday weighing the fate of McVeigh, who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.

The decorated former soldier, 29, has pleaded not guilty to charges of conspiracy, bombing and first-degree murder of the eight federal agents killed in the blast. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

The prosecution portrayed McVeigh as a right-wing fanatic driven to carry out the bombing by hatred of the government over the way federal agents handled a siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993.

The defence has argued that authorities arrested the wrong man. The defence team, led by Stephen Jones, tried to discredit key prosecution witnesses, attack the reliability of the government's scientific evidence and undermine eyewitnesses who identified McVeigh as the man who rented a truck the government says was used in the bombing.
The jury heard from 137 prosecution and 25 defence witnesses, and was given hundreds of exhibits.
Throughout, Federal Judge Richard Matsch exhorted jurors to avoid all publicity about the trial. On Friday he told them not to discuss the case outside their deliberations at the courthouse.
There was no indication how long the jury would take to reach a verdict.
The jurors were not allowed to take notes during the trial, but evidence was set up in an auxiliary courtroom so they could view it.

When Matsch put the case in the hands of the jurors, he reminded them: "The law does not permit jurors to be governed by sympathy, prejudice or public opinion. You're expected to carefully and impartially consider all the evidence, follow the law as stated by the court, and reach a just verdict."

The case moved along faster than anyone had expected, in part because Matsch kept firm control of the proceedings. "The case had the possibility of being unwieldy," said Denver attorney Andrew Cohen, who is following the trial. He called its speed "a tribute to the judge's organisational skills."
